note: experience as fundamental
why: Page says interest in the hard problem revived panpsychism, which addresses it directly, and that Chalmers explored panpsychism as viable.

note: 'the mind's i'
why: Page states Dennett co-edited and co-authored the 1981 collection The Mind's I with Hofstadter.

note: koch moved from NCC work with crick to working with tononi on IIT
why: Page supports only the biographical link through Koch; it does not say IIT grew out of NCC research.

note: many unconscious specialists
why: Baars and Franklin (2003) say the specialised processors of Global Workspace theory may correspond to Minsky's agents, citing The Society of Mind.

note: most of the mind is not the conscious part
why: Essay draws the parallel between Freud's unconscious and the largely unconscious System 1, and notes Kahneman studied Freud.

note: feeling grounded in body regulation
why: Seth (2013) says his model is related to Damasio's, both grounding selfhood in physiological condition, and adds top-down inference.

note: hoffman grants the resemblance but says his theory is not idealism
why: Hoffman writes that similar ideas exist in idealism, yet 'MUI theory is not idealism' and conscious realism is not Kant's idealism.

note: blackmore's illusionist account uses metzinger's self-model
why: Blackmore's reply to Frankish cites Metzinger (2009) for the self-as-observer representation; no page equates the no-self claim with illusionism.

note: leary found the book confirmed his psilocybin experience, then befriended huxley
why: Page's Influence section says this; it does not say Leary took the filtered-mind idea from Huxley.

note: non-classical physics in the brain
why: Page lists Pribram's holonomic theory and Penrose-Hameroff side by side as quantum approaches to mind; no influence is claimed.

note: minds running as software
why: Article on the simulation argument cites Permutation City as exploring life as a copy in a simulated world.

note: intelligence without experience
why: No page found linking Blindsight to illusionism; the novel treats consciousness as real but dispensable, a different thesis.

note: psi compared with soar and ACT-R
why: Bach's thesis compares the Psi theory with Soar and ACT-R and stresses differences; it does not say Psi builds on them.

note: maslow's hierarchy of needs reread as a hierarchy of purposes
why: Bach writes that Maslow's hierarchy of needs 'is better understood as a hierarchy of purposes'.

note: via dörner's psi theory, which takes up bischof's cybernetic psychology
why: Bach's thesis says Dörner's theory incorporates Bischof's ideas and cites Bischof for feedback loops in psychology; the link is indirect.

note: emotions as modes of the whole system, not a lookup table
why: Bach's 2019 paper: MicroPsi does not implement emotions explicitly 'like in the classic OCC model'; they emerge from modulators.

note: philosophy of mind by designing working minds
why: Bach's thesis cites Sloman for the active design stance of a constructing engineer and among philosophers drawn to AI.

note: needs as feedback loops
why: Bach: motivation can be understood 'from the perspective of control theory and cybernetics', needs balanced in a homeostatic control system.

note: neural execution of scripts
why: The ReCoN paper cites Schank and Abelson for hierarchical scripts and offers a neural solution for executing them.

note: bach lists global workspace theory among views converging on his own
why: Bach names Baars's theory as one of several perspectives converging with his; he does not say he built on it.

note: the self is a representation, not an agent
why: Bach's 2019 paper refers to Metzinger 2003 for the argument that the self is a representation without agency.

note: conductor theory as an extension of the multiple drafts model
why: Bach writes his theory 'can be thought of as an extension to Dennett's multiple drafts model'; narrative gravity is not mentioned.

note: we experience the mind's model, not the thing in itself
why: No statement by Bach tying his model view to Kant was found; the thing-in-itself appears only in a paper by CIMC colleagues.

note: vervaeke calls the cave the first simulation theory; bach answers 'almost'
why: The cave is put to Bach by Vervaeke, not raised by him; elsewhere Bach reads Plato's forms as an embedding space.

note: bach's 'enlightened' stage is reached mostly by advanced buddhist meditators
why: Bach says stage six is found mostly in Buddhist meditators, but calls Buddhism limited to the inside view; no dependence stated.

note: the hard problem dissolves if experience belongs to a simulated character
why: Bach names Chalmers, calls the hard problem 'a bit of a misunderstanding', and places experience in the world the mind creates.

note: matter is not conscious; only a simulation can be
why: Bach finds panpsychism 'unsatisfying'; elsewhere he says physical things cannot be conscious, only representational structures can.

note: waking perception as a dream constrained by the senses
why: Bach calls every experience of reality a dream state, contrasts it with night and lucid dreams, and says daytime dreams are constrained by sensory input.

note: any cells can compute; morphogenesis and mind may share one algorithm
why: Bach credits Levin with these two ideas and extends them; 'cells running shared goals' is not his wording.

note: bach moves from dawkins's selfish genes to competing software agents
why: Bach cites Dawkins on genes and says the real invariant is software; he does not cite Dawkins's memes.

note: gods as shared archetypes
why: Bach uses the Greek gods as an example of gods as archetypes spanning many minds; an illustration, not a source he builds on.

note: the church as a collective agent; 1 corinthians 13
why: Bach describes Christianity as an agent with the Church as nervous system and quotes 1 Corinthians 13; analysis, not dependence.

note: gods as voices in the mind
why: Bach says gods are agents existing across people whose voice you hear in your mind, and that this theory is in Jaynes's book.

note: strong computationalism: reality itself computes
why: In the FLI episode on digital physics Bach says 'the universe is made from integers' and defends a computable foundation of physics.

note: computationalism as the heir of mechanism
why: Bach writes that computationalism replaced the intuitions of mechanistic philosophy, citing La Mettrie; his 37C3 talk names La Mettrie as a forerunner.

note: only what can be constructed exists
why: Bach endorses the constructivist programme, calls intuitionism its first formulation, and says truth requires constructing the object.

note: no completed infinities
why: Bach retells the contradictions that followed Cantor's infinite sets and concludes, via constructive mathematics, 'there are no infinities'.

note: nothing computes beyond turing
why: Bach's 'strong computationalism': no implementable language exceeds a finite automaton, and hypercomputational objects cannot exist.

note: the tractatus as a programme for a precise language
why: Bach admires the Tractatus as a project for a precise language of thought but says Wittgenstein found it could not be grounded.

note: love among the theological virtues
why: Bach reads Aquinas's divine virtues as policies for multi-agent systems; love is the discovery of shared higher purpose.

note: values derived from how agents work, not a pleasure calculus
why: Bach criticises utilitarianism's metric over hedonic states as unworkable for mutable minds, and calls it an unsuccessful repair of morality.

note: bach's reading of what language models are
why: Bach discusses what large language models are in this interview; that is commentary on them, not his work building on them.

note: shared a panel on machine sentience
why: Only the joint panel is documented; no page compares their accounts of models playing characters, and the panel content was not read.

note: cimc's whitepaper cites the report as ai welfare research
why: The whitepaper cites Butlin et al. only when describing Eleos AI; its own stance on behavioural tests is not attributed to them.

note: the institute's hypothesis rests on his conductor model, his functionalism and the idea that consciousness comes first
why: The hypothesis paper, co-written by Bach, states the conductor theory, functionalism, and consciousness as a prerequisite of learning.

note: IIT says an ordinary computer can never be conscious
why: Whitepaper: IIT holds a perfect digital simulation of a brain could lack consciousness, 'a direct rejection of functionalism'.
